Claim: In a 2025 US probability-panel survey, comfort with AI in financial services ranged from 62% for AI that flags fraud and freezes accounts to 20% for AI that approves or denies mortgages, both below non-financial AI uses such as traffic routing (80%).
Evidence: Consumer Reports/NORC AmeriSpeak, 4,073 US adults 18+, 12 Sep-16 Oct 2025, item 'Please tell us how comfortable or uncomfortable you would be with AI in each of these situations' (base: those for whom the situation applied): 62% at least somewhat comfortable with AI that flags potential fraud and freezes accounts if needed; 20% with AI that approves or denies mortgage applications | Same item, non-financial comparators (2025, same population): 80% at least somewhat comfortable with AI that tells you the fastest way to drive through traffic; 71% with AI-powered movie or show recommendations | Same survey, asked of those who said they had encountered each use (2025): 70% who encountered AI in a fraud alert felt generally positive, the only encounter type with a majority positive; 37% of those who experienced an automated credit decision felt generally positive | Method (2025): NORC AmeriSpeak probability-based panel, online n=3,842 and phone n=231, English and Spanish, weighted, margin of error +/-1.99 points; report published April 2026
Implication: A US bank should expect a clear task gradient in stated comfort, with fraud protection the easiest AI role to earn consent for and credit decisions among the hardest.
Caveats: Sponsor is Consumer Reports, an advocacy nonprofit whose framing stresses consumer protections; NORC, an independent research organisation, fielded it with disclosed method. Hypothetical comfort, not use. The two anchor tasks differ in stakes and in whether AI flags or decides, so task and stakes are confounded inside this instrument. Asks about financial companies generally, not banks, and has no provider comparison. Middle tasks (billing chatbot, loan-rate setting) appear only as chart labels and are not used. Full toplines sit at a separate CR URL not fetched.

Claim: In the same 2025 US survey, at least half of adults were at least somewhat uncomfortable with each of five financial actions an AI agent might take without per-action approval; comfort was highest (32%) for moving money between one's own accounts to avoid fees and discomfort highest (74%) for an agent applying for credit, and only 1% reported having used such an agent.
Evidence: Consumer Reports/NORC, 4,073 US adults, Sep-Oct 2025, base all respondents, item 'How comfortable or uncomfortable would you be with an AI agent doing each of the following on your behalf, without needing your approval each time?': 54% very and 20% somewhat uncomfortable with an agent applying for a loan or credit card when it decides you might need more credit | Same item (2025): transferring money between my accounts when it predicts I could avoid fees was the most accepted scenario, 32% somewhat or very comfortable; report summary states 56% to 74% were at least somewhat uncomfortable across the five scenarios (others: switching to a cheaper insurance or credit option, buying routine products, buying and selling investments) | Same survey (2025), item 'Have you ever used a financial service where AI made decisions or took actions on your behalf without following fixed rules you set up ahead of time?': 1% yes, 70% no, 29% unsure; report says most yes answers described routine automation such as overdraft protection and automatic transfers | Same survey (2025): 6% of AI users vs 4% of non-users very comfortable with an algorithm using car data to set an insurance premium, against 47% vs 25% for AI driving directions, so AI experience barely moved financial-AI comfort
Implication: Autonomous agent actions start from minority comfort even for the mildest money movement, so a bank should launch agents permission-gated and treat the low-stakes own-account transfer as the first candidate.
Caveats: Same sponsor and fielder as T1-01. Mixed on H1: a task ordering exists (own-account transfers above credit applications) but discomfort is broad across all five tasks, so the dominant signal is resistance to unapproved autonomy rather than to particular tasks. Scenarios are hypothetical because almost nobody has used a true agent. No provider comparison.

Claim: Asked what would make them more willing to let AI handle money, US and UK consumers most often name control and protection conditions (human override, per-action approval, reimbursement, undo, protective rules, proven accuracy) and rarely the provider's identity, but neither survey tests whether these conditions close task-level gaps.
Evidence: Consumer Reports/NORC, 4,073 US adults, Sep-Oct 2025, base all, multi-select 'What, if anything, would make you more comfortable with AI agents making financial decisions on your behalf?': speak with a human at any time to override or stop the agent 47%; approve each action before it happens 45%; fully reimbursed if the agent made a mistake 44%; easily undo any action 43%; a government agency regulates it 23%; nothing would make me comfortable 25% | FCA-commissioned Yonder online panel, 5,026 UK adults with a day-to-day bank account, April 2026, 'Which of the following would make you more likely to use AI tools for managing your money and financial services?' (ranked top three): clear rules protecting me if something went wrong 32%; proven track record of accuracy and reliability 30%; easily opt out or speak to a human 22%; offered by a financial services provider I already trust 13%; none 24% | Same FCA survey (2026), top-three barriers to using AI for managing money: do not trust what it will do with my information or data 59%; prefer to speak to a human 42%; can manage finances without outside help 42%; do not trust the information it provides 41%
Implication: Recourse, approval and human override are the levers customers say they want, and incumbency is a weak lever by their own account, so a bank should design and test these controls rather than rely on its brand to carry AI trust.
Caveats: Two separate surveys reported side by side, not combined. Stated hypothetical conditions, not behaviour: neither survey shows comfort actually rising once the condition is offered, so the H1 counter-claim that task gaps collapse under control is untested. FCA percentages were mapped to labels by chart order in the extracted PDF. Provider trust was one of about a dozen options with a top-three cap, which may understate it. FCA asks about AI tools generally, not bank AI. Also bears on H2 (drivers).

Claim: In an April 2026 FCA-commissioned UK concept test, stated willingness to use AI financial services fell from 36% when AI recommends to 30% when it acts with permission each time to 20% when it acts autonomously, and the drop with autonomy appeared in every one of five task concepts, with moving money the least popular task.
Evidence: FCA/Yonder, 5,026 UK adults with a day-to-day bank account, April 2026, each respondent saw 1 of 5 concept sets at 3 autonomy levels in sequence, item 'How likely would you be to use something like this, if it were available to you now?': definitely or probably use 36% (Level 1, AI reviews and recommends), 30% (Level 2, acts asking permission each time), 20% (Level 3, acts on pre-set instructions or goals); would not use 52%, 56%, 68% | Same item by concept, Level 1/2/3, from chart data labels (2026): moving money between your accounts 24/21/16; switching financial products 39/31/21; managing insurance 46/39/24; borrowing and credit 35/31/21; saving and investing 34/28/20; report text calls reviewing insurance the most attractive use case and AI with direct control over moving money the least popular | Same item among those who have used AI, n=3,473 (2026): 48%, 40%, 28%; report states a segment rejects the concepts at all autonomy levels, so exposure alone may not overcome resistance
Implication: Both the task and the degree of autonomy move willingness, and autonomy moves it at least as much, so a bank should sequence AI features from advise to act-with-approval to autonomous within each task and treat autonomous money movement as the hardest case.
Caveats: Regulator-commissioned research with disclosed method, classed Observed/Administrative per the brief, but it measures stated intention to use a described concept, not behaviour. Concepts were assigned between subjects and levels shown in fixed sequence, so order effects are possible. Task is crossed with concept wording, so task and wording cannot be separated. Insurance review was the favourite, which cuts against a simple low-stakes-is-easier reading. UK jurisdiction; direction likely transfers to the US, levels may not.

Claim: In the April 2026 FCA survey, 16% of UK account holders already used AI for at least one personal-finance task, mostly to summarise, explain and compare, with use higher in advice-heavy areas (investing, debt, tax), and most who used it checked the output against other sources rather than following it.
Evidence: FCA/Yonder, 5,026 UK adults with a day-to-day bank account, April 2026, item 'Do you currently use an AI-enabled tool to assist you with, or do, tasks in any of these areas?': 16% use AI for at least one personal-finance task, 23% among those already using AI elsewhere; 67% use AI for any purpose | Same report executive summary (2026): current use is mainly assistive (summarise, explain, simplify, compare) and is higher for investing, debt management and tax planning, areas where consumers traditionally sought advice; product-level shares appear only in charts and are not quoted | Among those who used AI for financial products, n=630, item 'When you used AI to assist you, what did you do afterwards?' (2026, chart labels by product): 62% to 80% compared AI advice with other sources; 14% to 25% followed the AI's suggestion; 2% to 6% ignored it | Item 'In general, would you be willing to give an AI real time access to your banking and financial data?' (2026): 13% yes among all consumers, 18% among current AI users
Implication: Actual use already reaches advice-like tasks that stated-preference surveys say customers reserve for humans, so a bank should expect customers to use outside AI for these tasks regardless and compete as the verified, protected place to do it.
Caveats: Self-reported use, not logged behaviour. Does not separate bank-provided AI from general-purpose assistants. Higher use in advice-heavy areas sits against stated preferences for human advice in other instruments (T1-06), which suggests a stated-versus-revealed gap but is not a same-person comparison. UK jurisdiction.

Claim: In a February 2026 Ipsos poll for TD, most Canadians preferred AI for routine servicing (fee questions, balances, password resets) while most preferred human-only handling for loan approvals and financial and retirement planning.
Evidence: Ipsos online poll for TD Bank, 2,501 Canadians 18+, 17-23 Feb 2026, weighted to Census, credibility interval +/-2.4 points: prefer AI-powered solutions for quick answers about fees or products 59%, checking account balances and routine transactions 55%, resetting passwords or fixing login issues 52% | Same poll (2026): comfortable with AI applied behind the scenes to track spending 55% and to calculate credit scores 53%; 50% comfortable using AI-enabled budgeting tools themselves | Same poll (2026): prefer human-only assessments for approvals for loans or other financial products 55%, financial planning advice 55%, retirement planning advice 53%; 71% trust human intelligence more than AI; 59% comfortable with banks using AI with meaningful human oversight
Implication: Routine servicing is the safest first home for bank AI, with human-only paths kept visible for lending and planning; Canada's banking structure makes this a close analogue for the US but the source is a bank's own poll.
Caveats: Sponsor is TD, a bank with an AI product agenda, so the survey exists partly because a bank went looking for task-level comfort; rated Low on that basis. Ipsos fielded it with disclosed n, dates and weighting, but the questionnaire is unpublished and wording is only as paraphrased in the press release. 'Prefer AI' and 'prefer human-only' are forced preferences with a third option (AI-supported human help) only partly reported. Note 53% are comfortable with AI calculating credit scores while 55% want human-only loan approvals, consistent with an assist-versus-decide line rather than a pure task line.

Claim: In a late-2022 British probability survey of 17 AI uses, AI assessing loan-repayment risk was one of 10 uses where perceived benefit outweighed concern, while AI assessing job eligibility was one of 5 where concern outweighed benefit, and only 35% had heard of loan-risk AI.
Evidence: Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, fielded by Kantar on its Public Voice random probability panel, 4,010 adults in Great Britain, Nov-Dec 2022 (ChatGPT released two weeks into fieldwork), items 'To what extent do you think that the use of this technology will be beneficial?' and a parallel concern item: benefit outweighed concern for 10 of 17 uses including assessing risk of repaying a loan; concern outweighed benefit for 5 including AI for assessing job eligibility | Loan-repayment-risk benefits selected (2022), item 'Which of the following, if any, are ways you think the use of this technology will be beneficial?': applying for a loan faster and easier 52%; less likely than banking professionals to discriminate 39%; less human error 37%; more accurate than banking professionals 29% | Loan-repayment-risk concerns selected (2022): banking professionals may rely too heavily on the technology 51%; harder to understand how loan decisions are reached 49%; difficult to know who is responsible if it makes a mistake 43%; personal information shared with third parties 37% | Awareness (2022), 'Before today, had you heard of the use of AI technologies for...': 35% for assessing loan repayment risk vs 93% for facial recognition to unlock phones
Implication: Even a mostly unaware public weighed AI credit assessment as net-beneficial but flagged opacity and accountability, so a US bank should pair any AI credit decision with explanation and a named accountable human.
Caveats: Pre-generative-AI vintage (2022), not current state. UK credit and adverse-action regime differs from the US. Compares a credit use with non-financial uses rather than a menu of banking tasks; the two eligibility uses (loan risk net-positive, job eligibility net-negative) are both high-stakes, so the contrast reflects domain or familiarity more than stakes. Net-benefit means are only in a chart. Contrasts with the US 2025 finding that only 20% were comfortable with AI deciding mortgages (T1-01): different wording, country and year, not combined. A 2024/25 wave exists but its financial items were not retrieved.

Claim: In a February 2024 US split-sample experiment, labelling a personal-finance statement as AI-generated rather than from a financial professional changed trust little or not at all for some statements and lowered it for others, and the AI-versus-professional gap varied more by statement and respondent group than by a uniform AI penalty.
Evidence: FINRA Investor Education Foundation, SSRS Opinion Panel probability-based, 1,033 US adults, 16-19 Feb 2024, margin of error +/-3.6, AAPOR3 response rate 2.4%, item 'Please indicate how much you trust or distrust this information' with source randomly named as AI or an individual financial professional: stock-vs-bond forecast trusted by 34% (AI) vs 33% (professional); portfolio allocation statement 30% (AI) vs 37% (professional) | Same study (2024): homeownership statement more trusted from the professional (chart labels 65% vs 57%, chi-square p=0.03); savings-before-debt statement similarly trusted by source per report text | Subgroups (2024, report text): men trusted the stock forecast more from AI (37% vs 27%); respondents with higher self-assessed knowledge 48% AI vs 34% professional; Black respondents trusted the homeownership statement more from AI (71% vs 49%) but the savings statement more from the professional (69% vs 48%) | Same survey (2024), 'Which of the following information sources do you use when making financial decisions?': financial professionals 63%, friends and family 56%, financial management apps 25%, AI 5%
Implication: For informational content the AI label carries no uniform penalty and the content and customer segment matter more, so a bank should test AI-delivered information by segment rather than assume blanket distrust.
Caveats: Sponsor is FINRA's investor-protection foundation, not a vendor. Tests trust in information statements, two of them contestable, not delegation of an action. Response rate 2.4%. Generic 'artificial intelligence' label fielded before most consumers used chat assistants. The 65% vs 57% homeownership figures are chart labels. Single wave.

Claim: In a spring 2026 Gallup survey, few US adults had strong confidence in AI as a source of financial guidance (3% a great deal; no more than about 30% at least some), yet 18% of those who sought financial guidance in the past year had used AI tools for it, so advice is not a task customers simply refuse to give to AI.
Evidence: Edward Jones and Gallup Financial Fulfillment study, Gallup Panel self-administered web survey, 5,075 US adults 21+, 20 Mar-6 Apr 2026, margin of error +/-1.8: no more than three in 10 have at least some confidence in AI as a source of financial guidance, 3% a great deal; 79% have at least some confidence in the expertise of financial advisors (exact item wording not printed) | Same survey (2026), among adults who sought financial guidance in the past year: own internet research 73%, family 35%, professional financial advisors 32%, news, media or social media 26%, friends 23%, artificial intelligence tools 18% | Same survey (2026), by generation: about one in four Gen Z adults and millennials used AI for financial guidance vs 7% of baby boomers; at least some confidence in AI tools 32% Gen Z, 36% millennials, 27% Gen X, 15% boomers
Implication: A meaningful minority already takes money guidance from AI tools despite weak confidence, so a bank should assume advice-like AI use is happening outside its walls and compete on being the safer channel.
Caveats: Sponsored by Edward Jones, an advice firm with an interest in the advisor-versus-AI comparison; Gallup fielded it with disclosed method. Use is self-reported and among guidance-seekers only, while confidence is among all adults, so the two are on different bases and use does not exceed confidence (about 18% use vs up to 30% some confidence). 'Financial guidance' is broad and 'AI tools' is not defined on the page. Single wave.

Claim: US bank chatbot and virtual-assistant use is mass-scale but concentrated in routine servicing, and satisfaction and willingness drop where tasks become complex or contested (problems, disputes, fraud, product questions).
Evidence: CFPB report Chatbots in Consumer Finance (2023): over 98 million users, about 37% of the US population, engaged with a bank's chatbot in 2022, projected to 110.9 million by 2026 (CFPB cites an Insider Intelligence estimate); all top-10 US commercial banks use chatbots of varying complexity | Bank of America press release, March 2026 (company disclosure): 20.6 million users interacted with Erica nearly 700 million times in 2025; over 3.2 billion client interactions since 2018; no split between informational and transactional use | J.D. Power 2026 US Digital Banking and Credit Card Mobile App Satisfaction Studies, 18,028 US retail bank and credit card customers, Jan-Mar 2026: only 28% of national bank and credit card app customers use virtual assistants; users score 736, 18 points above non-users; satisfaction drops sharply when users try to resolve problems, dispute charges or identify fraud | Deloitte survey of 2,027 US bank customers, January 2025: 37% never used a bank chatbot; use mainly for technical support (60%) and existing-account inquiries (53%); of those who used chatbots for product inquiries, 82% would not use them for that again and 46% would visit a branch instead; 74% favored human agents over chatbots for these interactions
Implication: Customers readily use bank assistants for lookups and simple servicing, but this says nothing about letting AI move money, and the experience fails exactly where stakes rise, so disputes, fraud and product advice need better assistants or human routing first.
Caveats: The CFPB adoption count is a commercial (Insider Intelligence) estimate relayed by the regulator, counts anyone who 'engaged', and is 2022 data. Erica figures are Bank of America company disclosure about a largely scripted assistant: interactions are usage, not trust, and not agentic. J.D. Power sells research to banks and does not print item wording. Deloitte is a consultancy selling AI and banking work, fielded the survey itself and does not disclose weighting; it is not sole support for any claim here. Usage can be forced when a bot is the only channel. Rated Low because no independent source with disclosed method supports the task contrast.

Claim: In incentivised investment experiments, lay participants delegated to or chose algorithms at least as often as human professionals, while their stated judgments and self-reported real-life delegation favoured humans, a stated-versus-revealed gap within the same studies.
Evidence: Holzmeister, Holmen, Kirchler, Stefan and Wengstrom, Innsbruck working paper 2019-21: 550 adults from a Statistics Sweden sample of the general working population, incentivised online allocation task, 4 Jan-10 Feb 2019, average pay about $30: delegation 37.9% to an investment algorithm vs 16.9% to a fixed-fee finance professional and 25.9% to an incentive-aligned professional (algorithm vs fixed fee MEM=0.210, p<0.001) | Same study, post-experiment survey (n=405, 2019): self-reported real-life delegation mean 3.36 to finance professionals vs 1.71 to investment algorithms (paired t-test p<0.001), the reverse of the experiment; authors note an algorithm built by researchers may be trusted more than one designed by a financial institution | Niszczota and Kaszas, PLOS ONE 2020, five Mechanical Turk studies, N=3,828: pooled robo-investment aversion in permissibility ratings d=-0.39 [-0.45, -0.32] (random effects -0.36); in the only incentivised study (Study 4, N=705) 52% chose a neural-network algorithm vs 48% a human (p=.27), with 47.8% choosing the algorithm for controversial stocks vs 56.5% for non-controversial (p=.021); in Study 5 (N=743, told performance was similar, not incentivised) 57.3% chose human advice | Germann and Merkle, Journal of Business Economics 2023 (abstract only): in a delegated-investing experiment, no sign of algorithm aversion; participants' inability to separate skill from luck slowed their migration to the algorithm
Implication: Stated discomfort with AI managing money is a poor predictor of what people choose when money is at stake, so a bank should test delegation features with real choices rather than infer refusal from attitude surveys, and watch values-laden decisions where aversion reappears.
Caveats: Pre-generative-AI (2019-2020 fieldwork); abstract allocation rules, not branded bank products; Sweden and MTurk (country not stated), not US bank customers; small real stakes. These experiments manipulate the type of agent, not the task, so they test the stated-versus-revealed counter-claim rather than task ranking directly. Holzmeister is a working paper; Germann and Merkle read at abstract level only. Aversion reappeared for morally controversial stocks, a content effect that partly supports task-dependence.

Claim: In lab experiments outside finance, people weighted or delegated to algorithms and AI more than to humans across objective and subjective tasks, and their reluctance to delegate applied about equally to human agents, pointing to a general preference for control rather than task-specific distrust of AI.
Evidence: Logg, Minson and Moore, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 151 (2019), online and lab samples: lay participants gave more weight to identical advice labelled algorithmic than human in weight estimation (Exp 1A, N=202), song-rank forecasts (1B, N=215) and romantic-attraction forecasts (1C, N=286); in a follow-up, weight on advice 0.34 (algorithm) vs 0.24 (person), F(1,669)=17.68, p<.001, d=0.33 | Same paper (2019): appreciation waned when people chose between the algorithm and their own estimate (Exp 3, N=403), and 70 US national security professionals relied less on algorithmic advice than 301 MTurk participants (Exp 4) | Ivanova-Stenzel and Tolksdorf, CRC TRR 190 Discussion Paper 558 (Dec 2025), TU Berlin students, n=95 hiring task and n=95 forecasting task, incentivised: delegation to AI and to human agents highly correlated (Kendall tau 0.44 and 0.46); 41% and 47% delegated more to the AI vs 10% and 12% more to the human; both agents outperformed participants yet were under-used
Implication: Resistance to letting AI act may be a control preference that applies to any agent, so a bank should preserve a visible way for customers to stay in charge rather than only proving the AI is competent.
Caveats: No financial tasks; low-stakes estimates, forecasts and hiring choices; MTurk and student samples. Advice weighting is not delegation of an action. Logg's fieldwork predates generative AI; Logg et al. also find aversion follows observed errors (consistent with Dietvorst 2015), which these designs mostly avoid. Ivanova-Stenzel is an unreviewed working paper and its task difference is confounded with design differences between the two experiments.

Claim: For consequential moral decisions, people judged machine decision-makers less permissible than humans even when outcomes were good, and only partly relented when the machine was limited to advising a human.
Evidence: Bigman and Gray, Cognition 181 (2018), nine studies on Amazon Mechanical Turk with US and Canadian participants (Study 1 N=242): machines rated less permissible than humans for life-and-death decisions in driving, legal, medical and military scenarios, including when outcomes were positive | Study 7 (N=100, medical decision): 4 chose the machine alone, 32 the human doctor alone, 64 the doctor advised by the machine; the authors describe Studies 7 and 8 as relatively inconclusive | Study 9 (medical): machine rated less permissible (M=2.49) than doctor (M=2.94), F(1,405)=14.36, p<.001; higher machine expertise reduced aversion only when the expertise advantage was made salient
Implication: For consequential banking decisions (adverse credit action, hardship, large irreversible transfers) a recommend-then-human-decides design is the safer default, with the caveat that this evidence is about moral stakes, not banking.
Caveats: No financial task; hypothetical vignettes; MTurk sample; pre-LLM 'machine'. Stakes are not manipulated inside the paper, so the support for H1 is by analogy: it shows an aversion tied to the moral weight of a decision, which is closer to the stakes counter-claim than to a task distinction.

Claim: The academic literature has not quantified how much the task itself moderates acceptance of algorithms: the one meta-analysis found excludes task-type comparisons, a systematic review finds task factors the least studied, and the main task-subjectivity study places financial advice on the objective side where aversion was absent.
Evidence: Capogrosso, Treffers and Welpe, HICSS-58 (2025), meta-analysis of 32 experimental studies and 89 effect sizes, N=32,525, Web of Science English-language studies Jan 2010-30 Nov 2023: interventions reduce algorithm aversion by g=0.23 (95% CI 0.14-0.32; prediction interval -0.36 to 0.82; I2=86.32%); context-targeted g=0.55 (k=15, N=1,714) vs algorithm-targeted 0.16 and human-targeted 0.21, differences called marginal; studies comparing aversion across task or product types were excluded | Mahmud, Islam, Ahmed and Smolander, Technological Forecasting and Social Change 175 (2022), systematic review of 80 empirical studies: abstract states very little attention has been given to task and high-level factors | Castelo, Bos and Lehmann, Journal of Marketing Research (2019), via a Boston University Susilo Institute summary: algorithms trusted and used less for tasks perceived as subjective (dating) than objective (financial advice); in a Facebook ad field test there was no difference in clicks between human and algorithmic financial advice while human dating advice was preferred
Implication: No published estimate says how much 'which banking task' matters relative to stakes, framing or user traits, so a bank should not treat task-by-task comfort rankings as settled and should measure its own customers.
Caveats: Capogrosso was read in full but does not test H1. Mahmud is abstract-only (publisher 403). Castelo rests on a university research-centre summary because the journal paper was blocked; study sizes not verified. Literature is mostly lab, MTurk and pre-2024. Mixed because the only task-moderator evidence (subjectivity) supports task-dependence in general but places finance on the low-aversion side.

Claim: In a small 2026 study with a real AI agent, trust was lowest and demand for prior approval highest for sending an email on the user's behalf, not for the task framed as highest-stakes, suggesting that outward-facing actions without a preview drive withdrawal more than nominal stakes.
Evidence: Pochampally, An and Chen (Virginia Tech), arXiv 2607.18257 (2026): N=20 undergraduate computer-science students used the open-source OpenClaw agent on five tasks within subject (file retrieval, email drafting and sending, comparative recommendation, schedule planning, submission readiness check), plus a 64-student screening survey | Same study (2026), 1-5 scales: email sending trust M=3.10 and approval preference M=4.65 vs file retrieval trust M=3.90 and approval M=2.85; trust differed across tasks, Friedman chi-square(4)=16.08, p=.003 | Same study (2026): the submission check, framed as the highest-stakes task, produced trust and approval scores comparable to low-stakes tasks; participants reported regret when the agent acted without a preview even when its output was rated successful
Implication: For an agent that moves money, a preview-and-confirm step before any outward-facing action may matter more than which task it is, which a bank can test before assuming task type is the key variable.
Caveats: N=20 computer-science students at one university; fixed task order; one agent; unreviewed preprint; no financial task. The paper codes both the email and the submission check as irreversible, so reversibility does not by itself explain the gap; privacy, visibility and stakes are bundled. Mechanism evidence only, not a bank-customer estimate.

Claim: In 2026 Ipsos data, 9% of AI-aware consumers across 15 markets said they already let AI make purchases autonomously and 52% would not, and only 15% of US adults would give AI full purchasing autonomy, with the rest requiring approval or conditions tied to product and cost.
Evidence: Ipsos Market Essentials, 8,500 adults under 75 in 15 countries, February-April 2026; base 7,954 consumers aware of AI tools; question: have you used or would you consider using AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Copilot) for any of the following shopping-related activities (actual usage / would consider / would not use): have AI automatically purchase items 9% / 24% / 52%; monitor prices and auto-buy when they drop 12% / 42% / 35%; research products before buying 27% / 43% / 22% (Ipsos Views 2026) | Ipsos AI in Spending and Finance Poll, 1,500 US adults aged 18-65, interviewed 8 February 2026: just 15% would give AI full purchasing autonomy and 85% require outright approval or conditions based on product and cost; 57% want to see the AI's reasoning every time it makes recommendations; only 4% of Gen X and boomers permit fully autonomous purchasing (Ipsos Views 2026) | Same US poll, Figure 3, among those who would let AI purchase depending on product or cost (n=557), purchase value they would allow: under $10 22%, $10-49 26%, $50-99 23%, $100-249 16%, $250+ 8%; the paper's text reads this as 48% allowing purchases under $50 without approval, 16% over $100 and 8% at $250+ (Ipsos Views 2026) | Same paper, generational profiles: Gen Z 48% and boomers 69% explicitly reject autonomous purchasing; the US shows 9% actual use of autonomous purchasing with 32-45% openness (Ipsos Views 2026)
Implication: Consumers separate letting AI research from letting it buy, and accept buying mainly at low value with approval and visible reasoning, so a bank launching payment agents should start with small, approved, reversible actions and show the agent's reasoning.
Caveats: Ipsos white paper is marketing content aimed at brands and retailers; the US poll method is limited to an endnote (n=1,500, one day, ages 18-65, mode and weighting not stated). Retail shopping, not bank payments or bank-provided agents, and no provider comparison. The global base is AI-aware consumers only, so it overstates population rates, and the grid mixes current use with willingness. The value figures are internally inconsistent in the paper: Figure 3 bins are not monotone (peak at $10-49) and the text's 16% over $100 matches only the $100-249 bin; the figure values are reported as printed. Gen Z rejection runs against the common Gen Z trusts AI more claim. Added in the T3 recovery pass; mapped down to Low because the US method is thin.

Claim: Richer explanations of AI credit decisions raise consumers' confidence and sense of understanding but do not raise, and can lower, their ability to spot a wrong decision.
Evidence: FCA Research Note (Feb 2025), online RCT, 8,860 UK adults via Prolific, 5 hypothetical credit scenarios, 4 explanation genres (data-centric control vs features-based, combination, combination plus decision rule): control judged decisions correctly 82% of the time; treatment genres were 3 to 7pp lower; on an erroneous decision (Scenario 5) 51% of control challenged it vs 11 to 20pp fewer in treatment arms | Same RCT, attitudes: 62% of control said the information was sufficient, rising by 12pp in treatment arms (printed as 'between 12 and 12pp'); 72% of control were confident they could challenge an incorrect decision, 4 to 6pp more in treatment arms; 90%+ in all groups found the information helpful | John-Mathews ICIS 2021 short paper, French consumer panel, 400 adults (4 arms x 100), imagined bank AI refusing a EUR 1,500 loan, 7-point self-ratings plus right/wrong tests: post-hoc Shapley explanation raised perceived actionability to 4.46 from 3.97 (p<0.01) while tested actionability was 0.55 vs 0.49 (not significant); counterfactual explanation cut tested generalisability to 0.56 from 0.78 (p=0.02); a transparent points model raised tested actionability to 1.36 from 0.49 (p<0.01)
Implication: Do not treat customers saying an AI explanation is clear or satisfying as evidence that it builds calibrated trust; test whether customers can catch errors, and prefer simple rule-like reasons over post-hoc feature lists.
Caveats: FCA fieldwork year not printed; 2024 set from Feb 2025 publication. FCA control arm is another explanation, not no explanation. Hypothetical scenarios; Prolific sample; measures confidence and error detection, not a trust scale. Authors are FCA staff plus Warwick academics; not FCA policy. French study is a preliminary non-peer-reviewed short paper, 100 per arm, 2021, pre-generative-AI models; its trust row could not be extracted. High confidence rests on the FCA RCT; the French study is supporting only.

Claim: A single AI error sharply reduces reliance on and stated trust in AI advice, and explanations only partly cushion or repair the drop.
Evidence: Ben David, Resheff and Tron, AIES 2021: US MTurk adults (514 initial, 449 after screening, 365 in regression models) playing a lemonade-stand business game for real money (coins worth 2 US cents) with an AI 'financial advisor': adoption rose to 85.5% on day 7, fell to 61% on day 8 after one advisor failure and reached only 66% by day 10; drop was 41% with no explanation vs 16% (feature-based) and 21% (performance-based), both p<0.05 | Same study: accuracy (performance) explanation raised initial adoption to 73% vs an average 57% for other explanation types (p=0.029); human advisor vs unexplained AI showed no initial gap (56% vs 57.7%); offering an autopilot lifted adoption about 40% to a mean of 95% on day 11 | Han and Ko, Behavioral Sciences 2025, Korean adults with fund-investing experience (Embrain panel), Study 2 n=294, 5-item 7-point trust scale over three rounds: round x accuracy interaction F(2,554)=45.327, p<0.001, partial eta-sq 0.141; round x post-error explanation F(2,354)=16.573, eta-sq 0.086; round x financial literacy eta-sq 0.015 | Han and Ko Study 1 (n=189, 2x2 advisor x product risk): algorithmic advisor rated above human expert on trust (eta-sq 0.041), satisfaction (0.029) and reliance intention (0.060)
Implication: Design for the first wrong answer: show performance information and a reason at the moment of failure, because that is where trust is lost and where explanation measurably limits the loss.
Caveats: Ben David et al. was largely done at Intuit (sponsor interest); the task is a lemonade-stand production game labelled as financial advice, not investing or banking; stakes are cents; fieldwork year not printed (arXiv Jan 2021). Han and Ko: Korea only, vignette rounds, self-report, fieldwork year not stated (2025 is publication); effect sizes are different interaction terms and do not give a clean ranking of drivers. Germann and Merkle 2023 (row T2-03) found participants were NOT quicker to lose confidence in an algorithm after it erred, so error sensitivity may not be AI-specific.

Claim: Believed performance, not measured performance, drives reliance on algorithmic investment advice: aversion disappears when people think the algorithm is better, yet people can overpay for algorithmic advice that is no better.
Evidence: Niszczota and Kaszas, PLOS ONE 2020, five experiments, N=3,828 MTurk workers choosing human vs algorithmic fund manager: mean robo-investment aversion d=-0.39; in the incentivised Study 4 there was no general aversion (48% chose human, 52% algorithm); Study 5 with equal performance information showed aversion d=-0.30 | Germann and Merkle, Journal of Business Economics 2023 (abstract only), young adults tying incentives to a human fund manager or an algorithm: no sign of algorithm aversion, participants cared about returns, were not quicker to lose confidence in the algorithm after it erred, and inability to separate skill from luck slowed migration to the algorithm | Hanaki, Mao, Tse and Zhou, Osaka ISER DP 1268 (Dec 2024), pre-registered, 311 Osaka University students, Oct 2023 to Jun 2024, BDM willingness to pay (0 to 10) for stock-price forecasts: mean WTP 4.924 (algorithm), 4.171 (certified analysts), 2.987 (peers); algorithm advice was not better and did not improve accuracy; average payoff change -2.995 (algorithm) vs -2.051 (expert) in Task 1 and -3.175 vs -1.984 in Task 2
Implication: Performance is a real lever but only through what customers believe, so a bank should publish simple, honest performance evidence for its AI rather than assume customers will judge quality themselves or penalise poor quality.
Caveats: None are bank-customer samples: MTurk workers, young adults, Japanese students. Niszczota 2020 is pre-generative-AI. Germann and Merkle read from the RePEc abstract only (Springer paywall), so its sample size is unverified. Hanaki is an unrefereed discussion paper; the algorithm-over-expert WTP gap was only marginally significant. Vintage set to the newest fieldwork (Hanaki 2023-24); the others are 2020 and earlier.

Claim: In a loan-decision experiment, an appeal route and an explanation each raised perceived fairness substantially, while telling people a bank employee reviews uncertain AI decisions had no effect.
Evidence: Yurrita et al., CHI 2023 (thesis chapter 4 full text), 267 Prolific participants after exclusions (279 recruited), between-subjects explanations x human oversight x contestability x low/high stakes, fictional bank loan scenario: oversight on procedural fairness F(1,254)=0.004, p=0.95, Bayes factor 7.43 for the null; no oversight x contestability interaction (p=1.00) | Contestability on procedural fairness F(2,254)=20.60, p<0.001, partial eta-sq 0.14; explanations on informational fairness F(1,260)=74.21, p<0.001, partial eta-sq 0.22 | Overall fairness regression R-sq 0.46: procedural fairness beta 0.87 vs informational fairness beta 0.27
Implication: A 'reviewed by a human' label is not a trust lever on its own; a visible, usable way to contest an AI decision moved perceived fairness far more.
Caveats: Outcome is perceived fairness of a hypothetical decision, not trust or behaviour. Prolific sample, 60% with at least a bachelor's degree; nationality not reported in what was read. Oversight was one configuration (human reviews only low-confidence cases). ACM full text returned 403; figures come from the author's TU Delft PhD thesis chapter that reproduces the CHI 2023 paper. Fieldwork year inferred (2022). Merged from T2-A and T2-D.

Claim: In a field experiment at a German savings bank, customers followed AI investment advice more often when a human banker had the final say, but the effect worked as a reassurance cue rather than through belief in better advice.
Evidence: Yang, Bauer, Li and Hinz (forthcoming Management Science; arXiv June 2025): 137 customers recruited in two branches, Oct 4 to Nov 26 2021, 130 analysed, incentivised peer-to-peer loan investment decisions, randomised to AI-only, human-AI or human-labelled advice | Where advice was identical across conditions, share of decisions aligned with advice was 0.792 (human-AI, 168 observations) vs 0.683 (AI-only, 180 observations), p<0.05; effect strongest for riskier investments | Online follow-up, 100 German-speaking Prolific participants, Jul 30 to Aug 2 2024: the authors attribute the gain to human involvement acting as a peripheral cue raising affective appeal, not to belief in higher advice quality
Implication: A named human with the final say can raise uptake of AI advice, but a bank should read this as reassurance working, not as evidence that customers trust the AI itself.
Caveats: 130 customers at one German savings bank; endowed money, not own funds; preprint version read. Partly at odds with T2-04 (oversight label did nothing for fairness), but outcomes and the human role differ (behavioural advice-taking with a human final say vs fairness rating with low-confidence review). No bank sponsorship disclosed in the parts read.

Claim: People want control over AI and a small ability to modify an algorithm's output raises its use, but giving control does not reliably build trust: overriders of a robo-advice tool ended with lower trust in algorithms.
Evidence: Pew Research Center, American Trends Panel, 5,023 US adults, Jun 9-15 2025: 61% would like more control over how AI is used in their lives (up 6 points since 2024), 17% comfortable with their control; 13% say they have a great deal or quite a bit of control vs 57% not too much or none; 73% would let AI assist at least a little with day-to-day activities | Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey, Management Science 2018 (abstract only), three incentivised forecasting studies: participants were considerably more likely to use an imperfect algorithm when they could modify its forecasts, even slightly, and modification made them more satisfied, more likely to believe the algorithm superior and more likely to choose it later | Chak, Croxson, D'Acunto, Reuter, Rossi and Shaw, NBER WP 30616 (Nov 2022, abstract only), RCT of free robo-advice for loan repayment with representative UK consumers: robo-advice improved average repayment choices; vulnerable households tend to distrust it and override; non-adopters and overriders reported lower trust in algorithms at the end
Implication: Offer an edit, confirm or undo step on AI actions because demand for control is broad and modifiability raises use, but do not assume control alone raises trust among sceptical or vulnerable customers.
Caveats: Pew is general AI, not finance, and attitude only. Dietvorst 2018 and Chak 2022 read at abstract level only; samples and effect sizes not recorded. Dietvorst is a pre-generative-AI forecasting task; Chak is UK debt repayment. The Chak link between overriding and lower trust is correlational. Low because two of three supports are abstract-only.

Claim: US adults voice high distrust of companies' data and AI practices, yet most report low-effort privacy behaviour, and field-experiment evidence shows small incentives and frictions override stated privacy preferences.
Evidence: Pew, American Trends Panel, 5,101 US adults, May 15-21 2023: 70% have little or no trust in companies to make responsible decisions about how they use AI in their products; 81% say information companies collect will be used in ways people are not comfortable with; 73% feel little or no control over data collected by companies | Same Pew survey: 56% always, almost always or often click agree without reading privacy policies; 61% are skeptical anything they do will make much difference | Athey, Catalini and Tucker, NBER WP 23488 (2017, abstract only), MIT digital-currency field experiment: small incentives led people who say they care about privacy to give up private data easily; small navigation costs shaped privacy choices in sharp contrast with stated preferences; irrelevant reassuring privacy information made people less likely to avoid surveillance
Implication: Treat stated privacy concern as background, not as a predictor of who will refuse a bank AI feature; convenience and defaults will dominate in the moment, so the obligation to design honest consent sits with the bank.
Caveats: Pew items are about companies in general, not banks or financial AI, and behaviour is self-reported; fielded before the 2024-26 generative-AI wave. Athey et al. read at abstract level only, MIT student sample, 2017, data disclosure not AI use. T2-08 (DNB) finds privacy risk does lower app use, so the paradox is not total.

Claim: In a representative Dutch panel, perceived privacy risk lowered use of financial and payment apps and few users behaved paradoxically, indicating a privacy calculus rather than a pure paradox, though usage gaps by privacy attitude were modest.
Evidence: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper 794 (Brits and Jonker, 2023), CentERpanel, 7-22 Nov 2022, 2,465 respondents aged 16+ (77.5% response): paradoxical usage of the two financial app types was 7-12%; paradoxical non-usage of financial information apps was 28% | Mobile payment app use: 32% of privacy fundamentalists, 35% of pragmatists, 45% of privacy-unconcerned (35% overall); financial information apps: 5%, 4%, 4%; respondents classified 30% fundamentalists and 8% unconcerned | Regressions: app usage correlates positively with perceived benefits and negatively with privacy risk for all three app types; trust in the app provider correlates with adoption of mobile payment apps but not financial information apps
Implication: Privacy risk is a cost customers weigh against visible benefit, not a veto, so any bank AI that uses customer data should make its benefit concrete.
Caveats: Central-bank working paper (author views). Self-reported app use. Netherlands under PSD2; third-party data-sharing apps, not AI. Financial information app penetration only 4%, so those estimates are thin; the unconcerned group is small (8%).

Claim: Consumers directly exposed to a large data breach took protective steps such as monitoring and credit freezes but kept using their cards and did not switch lenders, and those exposed only to news of the breach barely reacted.
Evidence: Mikhed and Vogan, Philadelphia Fed Working Paper 17-06/R (Nov 2017): 2012 South Carolina Department of Revenue breach used as a natural experiment on credit-bureau data (5 percent random sample of US consumers with credit records, about 12 million) | Directly exposed consumers monitored files and froze credit reports but continued their regular use of existing credit cards and did not switch lenders; response of consumers exposed only to the news was negligible
Implication: A security incident is more likely to trigger protective behaviour than exit, so a bank should plan visible remediation rather than assume either loss or immunity of customer trust.
Caveats: Breach was at a state tax agency, not the consumer's bank and not AI. 2012 data. Fed working paper, authors' views. A university news page on bank-specific breaches and deposit outflows (Wang and Durongkadej 2025) was dropped: secondary summary with no effect sizes.

Claim: US confidence in banks as an institution is low and only a few points above large technology companies, so there is a thin institutional reservoir for bank AI to inherit.
Evidence: Gallup, telephone, Jun 2-26 2025, n=1,402 US adults, +/-4 points, 'how much confidence you, yourself, have in each one: a great deal, quite a lot, some, or very little': banks 30% great deal or quite a lot (White 32%, Black 25%, Hispanic 25%); large technology companies 24%; big business 15%; small business 70% | Same topline, recent trend for banks: 2019 30%, 2020 38%, 2021 33%, 2022 27%, 2023 26%, 2024 27%, 2025 30%; tech companies 2020 32%, 2021 29%, 2022 26%, 2023 26%, 2024 27%, 2025 24%
Implication: A bank cannot assume a large store of institutional goodwill to spend on AI, especially among Black and Hispanic customers, so AI trust has to be earned feature by feature.
Caveats: Institutional trust only; no AI item, so it says nothing about transfer by itself. Confidence in banks in general is not trust in one's own bank, which is usually rated higher. Gallup is independent. The Gallup trend web page was re-fetched but shows no numbers in text and was removed as a source.

Claim: In the largest same-sample US dataset found, trust that banks treat people fairly barely predicted interest in AI financial advice, while fintech use was a much stronger correlate.
Evidence: Reiter, Journal of Financial Planning, July 2026, analysing the 2024 National Financial Capability Study (n=18,904 US adults): 23% interested in AI-based financial advice | Trust item 'I trust that banks will treat me fairly' (1-7 scale): odds ratio 1.07; fintech use odds ratio 2.20 (strongest predictor); women's odds 34% lower than men's (OR 0.66) | Also positively associated: non-White identity, younger generations, bachelor's degree or higher, objective financial knowledge; working with a financial professional was not significant
Implication: Do not expect customers who trust the bank to be the early adopters of AI advice; existing fintech users and younger, more knowledgeable customers are likelier.
Caveats: Contradicts the strong version of a brand-halo account (bank AI trust is mostly inherited institutional trust); a positive OR of 1.07 does not rule out some transfer. Single fairness item as the trust measure; outcome is interest, an intention, not trust in a bank's AI. Trade-journal article, single author; regression read from the article, not the microdata. FINRA Foundation funds the NFCS, not this analysis.

Claim: In one 2025 US sample, more adults trusted businesses to act in society's best interest than trusted businesses to use AI responsibly, so general trust in business does not carry over fully to AI.
Evidence: Bentley-Gallup Business in Society 2025, Gallup Panel web survey, 3,007 US adults, May 5-12 2025, +/-2.8 points: 31% trust businesses 'some' or 'a lot' to use AI responsibly (a lot 3%, some 28%), up 8 points since 2024 and 10 since 2023; 69% little or no trust | Same survey: 43% have some or a lot of trust in businesses to act in society's best interest (up from 39% in 2022); federal government 31%, state and local government 50%, charitable and advocacy organisations 80%
Implication: Treat general trust in the bank as necessary but not sufficient, and plan for an AI-specific trust gap that has to be closed with visible responsibility measures.
Caveats: Businesses in general, not banks. The two items differ in construct and wording, so the 12-point gap is suggestive, not a transfer rate. Sponsor is Bentley University (business school); Gallup fielded it. The 31% figure was verified in the earlier fs-agent-landscape pass.

Claim: Small survey studies find firm reputation is associated with trust in banking chatbots and robo-advisers, but where relative weights are reported, attitude toward AI and perceived risk outweigh institutional factors.
Evidence: Kumalasari, Rubiyanti, Akbar and Miftahuddin (2026), PLS-SEM, n=111 Indonesian users with prior banking-chatbot experience: corporate reputation strongly influences trust in the chatbot; usefulness and trust predict intention (coefficients not shown in the abstract) | Senteio and Hughes, Journal of Financial Planning Aug 2024, n=86 US survey respondents (40 robo-adviser users, 46 human-adviser users) plus 10 interviews: reputation of the firm a significant positive influence on trust; model F(4,66)=8.47, p<.01; attitude toward AI carried the strongest weight of the four predictors | Alagarsamy and Mehrolia, Heliyon 2023, PLS-SEM, n=435 Indian banking-chatbot users: antecedents explained 38.6% of variance in chatbot trust; perceived risk beta -0.174, service quality 0.151, perceived usefulness 0.143, disposition to trust 0.136; structural assurance 0.087 (p=0.075, not significant); reputation not measured
Implication: Reputation probably helps a bank's AI start from a higher base, but these studies suggest product-level factors such as perceived risk and usefulness carry more weight, and none is a US bank-customer sample of adequate size.
Caveats: Small convenience samples (n=111 Indonesia; n=86 US investor-leaning advice users) and one moderate Indian sample; self-selected existing users; attitude and intention only. Kumalasari read at abstract level; fieldwork year not stated. Senteio individual coefficients not reported. Glikson and Woolley 2020 review (cited via a CMU news summary in T2-C) was dropped as not a primary source.

Claim: Demographic differences in trust of AI financial information are real but change direction by topic and subgroup, while confidence in AI for managing money rises steeply from older to younger generations.
Evidence: FINRA Foundation, SSRS Opinion Panel, 1,033 US adults, Feb 16-19 2024, +/-3.6 points, AAPOR3 response 2.4%, split-sample 'The following information was provided by an individual financial professional/artificial intelligence... how much do you trust or distrust this information': stock-vs-bond forecast trusted by 34% (AI) vs 33% (professional); higher self-assessed knowledge 48% (AI) vs 34% (professional); lower knowledge 25% (AI) vs 32% (professional); men 37% (AI) vs 27% (professional) | Same experiment: savings-vs-debt statement, Black respondents 69% (professional) vs 48% (AI); homeownership statement, Black respondents 71% (AI) vs 49% (professional); overall chi-square p for the four statements 0.03, 0.06, 0.05, 0.14; only 5% use AI when making financial decisions | Gallup with Edward Jones, 5,075 US adults, Mar 20 to Apr 6 2026: at least some confidence in AI's expertise for managing money 36% of millennials, 32% Gen Z, 27% Gen X, 15% baby boomers; 3% overall a great deal of confidence; 18% have sought financial guidance from AI tools
Implication: Plan for uneven acceptance by age, knowledge and background rather than one average customer, and test each AI feature with the groups least inclined to trust it before rollout.
Caveats: FINRA Foundation funded its poll; many subgroup comparisons on hypothetical statements, so single splits are fragile and direction flips by topic; AI asked about is unspecified 'artificial intelligence', not bank AI. Gallup/Edward Jones is sponsored by a financial-services firm; the age gradient may reflect exposure rather than age. No source compares demographic variance with design levers.

Claim: Trust in AI for banking information is far higher among people who already use generative AI and rises with AI experience among older adults, but the evidence is correlational and sponsor-produced.
Evidence: Deloitte Center for Financial Services (published Aug 2026), almost 2,600 US banking customers: trust when researching banking products, bank websites 79%, traditional search engines 67%, gen AI tools 49%, social media 28% | Same Deloitte survey: of about 1,700 who had used gen AI tools, 60% trusted the tools' accuracy vs 19% of those without gen AI experience; 72% concerned about sharing financial information with gen AI; 83% would feel anxious about an AI agent taking action on their finances without approval | AARP Research, online survey Jan 2025, 1,661 US adults incl. 1,148 aged 50+: 47% of those in their 50s know about and use AI and chatbots vs 25% of those over 70; respondents became more open to AI's merits once they learned about it and had some experience
Implication: Letting customers try low-stakes AI features may move trust more than leaning on the brand, but a bank should test that with its own usage data before relying on it.
Caveats: Deloitte sells financial-services AI advisory work; field dates, fielding firm and question wording undisclosed; vintage set from Aug 2026 publication. The user/non-user gap is likely selection (people who like AI use it). AARP is an advocacy organisation; its experience claim is descriptive. Consistent with the counter-hypothesis that familiarity dominates other drivers (see also fintech use OR 2.20 in T2-11), but nothing here ranks it against other drivers.

Claim: In a September 2020 US survey, consumers trusted traditional financial institutions most and big tech least to safely store their personal financial data, with fintechs in between.
Evidence: NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations special module, September 2020, n=1,361 US household heads; question asked how much respondents trust each counterparty to safely store their personal data (bank transaction history, geolocation or social media data) on a 1 (no trust at all) to 7 (complete trust) scale: traditional FIs median 5, about 60% scored 5 or higher, over 75% scored 4 or higher (BIS Bulletin 42, 2021) | Same survey: fintechs (examples given: PayPal, Venmo, Quicken Loans) and government agencies median 4, about 25% scored 5 or higher and about 25% scored 2 or lower (BIS Bulletin 42, 2021) | Same survey: big techs (Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google) median 2, three quarters scored 1-3, over one third no trust at all, 12% scored 5 or higher, 1.4% complete trust (BIS Bulletin 42, 2021) | Same survey: respondents aged 60+ trust traditional FIs more and fintechs and big techs significantly less than younger cohorts (age values shown only in a chart); minority respondents rate traditional FIs lower than non-Hispanic whites (average 4.2 vs 4.7) and big techs somewhat higher (BIS Bulletin 42, 2021) | Same survey: a quarter of respondents said Covid-19 made them less willing to share data; of these, nearly half became less willing to share with big techs (55% for minority respondents, 56% for older cohorts), fintechs showed a similar but lower pattern, and there was only a modest increase in the share less willing to share with traditional FIs (BIS Bulletin 42, 2021)
Implication: For anything that touches transaction data a bank starts with a clear stated-trust lead over big tech and a smaller one over fintech, but the lead is thinner among younger and minority customers, which is where migration would start.
Caveats: Central-bank research (BIS, NY Fed, SNB, Yale authors), no commercial sponsor. Measures trust to safeguard data, not trust in AI or in a provider acting for the customer. Single 2020 wave during the pandemic; no later wave of the counterparty ranking was found, so the trend in the gap is unknown. Sample skews older and whiter than the population (34% aged 60+ vs 22%; 80% non-Hispanic white vs 63%), which likely inflates the bank lead. Generic counterparty classes, not the respondent's own bank. Recovery pass: the Covid item is a self-reported change within the single 2020 wave, not a second wave, so it shows the gap widening under a shock by respondents' own account, not a measured trend.

Claim: US confidence in banks has stayed slightly above confidence in large technology companies since Gallup began asking about tech in 2020, and the gap closed in 2023-2024 before reopening in 2025-2026 as confidence in tech fell to a series low; both are under 30%.
Evidence: Gallup Confidence in Institutions, question: how much confidence do you have in each institution, a great deal, quite a lot, some or very little; share great deal or quite a lot, US adults. 2026 (June 1-15, telephone, n=1,001, MOE +/-4): banks 28% (10 + 18), large technology companies 20% (9 + 11) (Gallup 2026 topline) | Same series, trend table in the 2026 topline, banks vs tech companies: 2020 38 vs 32; 2021 33 vs 29; 2022 27 vs 26; 2023 26 vs 26; 2024 27 vs 27; 2025 30 vs 24; 2026 28 vs 20 (Gallup 2026 topline) | 2025 (June 2-26, telephone, n=1,402 incl. Black and Hispanic oversamples, weighted): banks 30% (11 + 19), large technology companies 24% (9 + 15) (Gallup 2025 topline) | Gallup 2026 release: confidence in large technology companies has fallen from 32% in 2020 to a new low of 20%, and those with very little or no confidence in tech rose from 32% in 2025 to 41%; banks are seven points above their historical low (the topline trend shows a 21% bank low in 2012) (Gallup 2026 release)
Implication: Big tech is not gaining institutional confidence at banks' expense, but a bank's edge is a few points on a low base, so bank AI cannot rely on institutional goodwill to win a contest with tech-branded agents.
Caveats: Independent pollster, no sponsor interest. Generic institutions, not money-handling providers; confidence is not trust to hold money or to act as an agent. The gap was zero in 2023 and 2024, so the bank advantage is not stable; it reopened mainly because tech fell, not because banks rose (banks fell from 38% in 2020 to 28%). Year-to-year moves of 2-4 points sit within the +/-4 margin of error. The trend table labels the item tech companies while the questionnaire lists large technology companies.

Claim: Half of US households use a nonbank payment app with a stored balance, but almost all of them keep a bank account and most banked users do not use the app for core account functions; distrust of banks keeps only a small slice of households unbanked. This is task migration (payments), not primary-relationship migration.
Evidence: FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households, June 2023, almost 30,000 households; question: do you or anyone in your household use any online payment services with an account feature that allows you to receive and store money in the account (examples PayPal, Venmo, Cash App; not Zelle): 49.7% of households in 2023 vs 46.4% in 2021; 51.0% of banked vs 20.1% of unbanked households (FDIC 2023 report) | Same survey: 33.5% of banked households using these services used them for at least one core transaction (pay bills, receive income, save or keep money safe) vs 71.5% of unbanked users; use was 68.5% among households aged 25-34 vs 25.1% aged 65+ (FDIC 2023 report) | Same survey: 4.2% of households (about 5.6 million) were unbanked in 2023 vs 4.5% in 2021 (difference not statistically significant); 95.8% were banked (FDIC 2023 executive summary) | Same survey: among unbanked households, don't trust banks was the second-most cited main reason (15.7% in 2023, 13.2% in 2021, 16.1% in 2019), behind not having enough money for minimum balances (23.3%) (FDIC 2023 executive summary)
Implication: Expect payment-type tasks, and AI that performs them, to be contested by nonbanks among younger households while the deposit account stays at the bank; the account relationship, not the task, is the asset to defend.
Caveats: Regulator survey with Census Bureau, no sponsor interest. Household-level use, not individual, volume, dollar share or primacy. Measures behaviour, not trust, and nothing about AI. Nonbank use is rising (46.4% to 49.7%) so the task share is still moving. Does not compare trust across provider types. Merges T3-A finding 3 and T3-B finding 1 (same survey).

Claim: Nonbank-led buy now, pay later grew quickly to tens of millions of US users by 2023 but remained about one percent of credit card spending volume, and a big-tech entrant (Apple) quit its own BNPL product within about a year: task-level credit migration that has not displaced bank cards.
Evidence: CFPB market report (December 2025), data from six large BNPL lenders estimated at about 40% of the point-of-sale financing market: 53.6 million consumers took out at least one BNPL loan in 2023, up 12% on 2022; number of loans up 23% and inflation-adjusted dollars up 26% (CFPB 2025) | Same report: the CFPB says the user count is likely overstated because lenders cannot see a user's loans at other lenders (CFPB 2025) | Same report: the BNPL data represent approximately one percent of total credit card spending volume in 2023 (CFPB 2025) | Same report: a large new entrant in March 2023 discontinued its proprietary product about a year later; the CFPB footnote cites an AP report naming Apple (CFPB 2025)
Implication: Nonbanks can take a narrow, convenient credit task at checkout, so a bank should expect agentic checkout and payment tasks to be contested even while the core card relationship holds.
Caveats: Lender-reported aggregate data from six firms, not a representative sample, with double counting of users. Measures adoption, not trust. The one percent comparison is the CFPB's own framing. Data are for 2023 though published in 2025. BNPL is classed here under Credit Decisions because it is an extension of credit; the task migrated is point-of-sale financing.

Claim: After the 2016 Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal, US counties more exposed to Wells Fargo showed lower reported trust in banks and a small shift of mortgage borrowers to fintech lenders, with no change in total bank deposits.
Evidence: Yang (working paper, May 16 2021), difference-in-differences on HMDA mortgage data with county exposure measured by Wells Fargo share of 2015 branch deposits: a one standard deviation rise in exposure raised the probability of choosing a fintech lender by 0.15 percentage points, a 2% increase on the 7.6% average (Yang 2021) | Same paper, Gallup individual data 2015-2018: a one standard deviation rise in exposure cut the probability of reporting trust in banks by three percentage points, a 10% decrease on the 29.6% average (Yang 2021) | Same paper: exposure had a minimal effect on bank deposits; deposits may have shifted from Wells Fargo to other banks but total banking-sector deposits did not change (Yang 2021) | UC Davis release on the published Journal of Financial Economics version: customers in more exposed areas were on average 4% more likely to use non-bank lenders after 2016, and fintech lenders' share rose from 2% of the market in 2010 to 8% in 2016 (UC Davis news release)
Implication: A bank trust shock costs shoppable, discrete products such as mortgage origination before it costs deposits, so a bank AI failure would most likely leak task-level share first.
Caveats: Working-paper estimates; the published JFE figures were not read and the university release gives a larger effect (4% vs 2%), so effect size is uncertain. County-level exposure, not individual switching. Fintech share was already rising. Deposit insurance confounds the deposit result. The shock was bank misconduct, not an AI failure. Peer-reviewed per the release; the journal page was not fetched.

Claim: In the spring 2023 runs on Silicon Valley Bank, Signature and First Republic, fully insured retail deposits did not run and at times grew, but uninsured and large depositors left within days, including a large share of consumer deposit dollars at two of the banks.
Evidence: FDIC staff study, Dissecting Depositor Flight (May 2026), core deposit-system data for March 6-24 2023: fully insured retail deposits did not run; between March 7 and March 17 they rose 46 percentage points at SVB while SVB total insured deposits fell 30 points, and rose 8 points at First Republic while its total insured deposits fell 7 (FDIC staff study 2026) | Same study: on March 6, fully insured retail deposits were about 2% of SVB deposits but held by 66% of SVB depositors; 13% of First Republic deposits, held by 96% of its depositors (FDIC staff study 2026) | Same study: between March 7 and March 17, more than half of consumer deposits left Signature (the study prints both 55% and 56%) and about one third (34%) left First Republic (FDIC staff study 2026) | Same study: top depositors were more likely to run even after accounting for insurance coverage and deposit type; most outflows left by wire (FDIC staff study 2026)
Implication: Deposit insurance, not trust alone, keeps small retail balances in place during a crisis, while larger and uninsured balances move in days, so a bank should not read retail deposit stickiness as proof of durable trust in its brand or its AI.
Caveats: FDIC staff views, not the FDIC's official position. Three business-heavy banks, not representative of retail banking. Measures behaviour by insurance status, not trust. Where the money went (other banks vs nonbanks) is not established here, so this says nothing direct about migration to fintech or big tech. The slice filed this as Contradicts; the consumer-deposit outflows make Mixed the honest reading.

Claim: Several big-tech attempts to provide bank-like accounts or credit were wound down or stayed bank-issued: Google shelved its Plex accounts in 2021, the Meta-backed Diem sold its payment technology to a bank in 2022, Apple ended its own BNPL product about a year after its March 2023 launch, and Apple Card is moving from Goldman Sachs to Chase as issuer.
Evidence: Google statement reported by the Boston Globe (wire report, October 1 2021): Google would focus on digital enablement for banks and other financial services providers rather than serving as the provider; Plex checking and savings accounts were to come from 11 partner banks, and the project was behind schedule per a person familiar with the matter (Boston Globe 2021) | Silvergate press release filed with the SEC (January 31 2022): Silvergate acquired Diem Group's blockchain payment network technology assets for $50 million in cash plus 1,221,217 shares, aggregate value $182 million at that day's close; no reason given for Diem's wind-down (Silvergate 8-K exhibit 2022) | CFPB BNPL market report (December 2025): a large March 2023 entrant discontinued its proprietary BNPL product a year later; its footnote cites an AP report naming Apple (CFPB 2025) | Chase release (January 7 2026): Chase to become Apple Card issuer, over $20 billion of card balances, transition expected in about 24 months, Mastercard remains the network (JPMorganChase 2026)
Implication: Big tech has so far chosen to distribute through chartered banks rather than hold the account, so the realistic threat to a bank is becoming an invisible back end behind a tech-branded front end rather than losing the regulated relationship.
Caveats: Corporate strategy decisions, not measured customer rejection; none of the sources attributes the outcome to consumer distrust (Plex: schedule and strategy; Diem: no reason stated, regulatory pressure is widely reported but not verified here; Apple Card: Goldman's exit). Two sources are company disclosures with an interest in favourable framing (Silvergate, JPMorganChase) and one is a news wire report, so the row is Low. Events span 2021-2026. The Chase release notes Apple Cash is provided by Green Dot Bank, another case of a big-tech front end on a bank charter.

Claim: A US fintech reports that two thirds of its 8.6 million active members use it as their primary financial relationship by its own definition, showing that some customers have moved the primary account relationship, not just tasks, to a nonbank brand, though the deposits sit at partner banks.
Evidence: Chime S-1 (SEC filing, 2025): 8.6 million Active Members at March 31 2025, an Active Member being one who initiated a money movement transaction in the last calendar month of the period (Chime S-1 2025) | Same filing: 67% of Active Members rely on Chime as their primary financial relationship, defined by Chime as 15 or more card purchases in the past calendar month or at least one qualifying direct deposit of $200 or more (Chime S-1 2025) | Same filing: Chime states it is a technology company, not a bank; banking services are provided by The Bancorp Bank, N.A. or Stride Bank, N.A., Members FDIC (Chime S-1 2025)
Implication: Primary-relationship migration to a fintech brand is real for a self-selected segment, so a bank should treat direct deposit and everyday debit spending as the signals that a customer's main relationship is at risk.
Caveats: Company disclosure in an IPO prospectus with an interest in showing engagement; primacy is Chime's own definition and is not comparable with Fed or FDIC measures. Active Members is not total accounts and no deposit share is given. Deposits are held at FDIC-insured partner banks, so trust may rest on the bank charter behind the brand. No independent neobank primacy data were found (see gaps). Sole source, so Low.

Claim: Use of general-purpose AI chatbots has become mainstream in the US, with ChatGPT use more than doubling since 2023, so AI labs now have a channel to most younger adults; Pew's published use categories do not include money or finance.
Evidence: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel, n=5,119 US adults, February 17-23 2026: 49% say they ever use AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot vs 33% in 2024 (2024 question asked only of those who had heard of chatbots) (Pew 2026) | Same survey: ChatGPT use 18% in 2023, 23% in 2024, 34% in 2025, 44% in 2026 (question wording changed in 2026); Gemini 24%, Copilot 17%, Meta AI 14%, Claude 6% in 2026 (Pew 2026) | Same survey: adults under 50 are about twice as likely as those 50+ to use ChatGPT (57% vs 28%) (Pew 2026) | Same survey, uses reported among all adults: search for information 42%, medical advice 20%, diet and fitness 20%, news 13%; no finance or money category appears in the published list (Pew 2026)
Implication: A bank cannot assume it is the first place customers under 50 take a money question, because an AI-lab assistant is already in their daily habits; but this is exposure, not trust for money tasks.
Caveats: Independent nonprofit pollster, no sponsor interest. Self-reported use of chatbots in general, not for money, and not trust. Wording changes between waves (2023-2025 asked only of those aware of ChatGPT), so the trend overstates comparability. The slice reported the age split as 18-29 vs 50+; the page gives under 50 vs 50+ (corrected). Finance may be in the Pew appendix tables, which were not checked.

Claim: Nearly one in five US adults who sought financial guidance in the past year used AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude for it, but no more than three in ten adults have even some confidence in AI's financial expertise, far below the 79% who have some confidence in financial advisors.
Evidence: Gallup and Edward Jones, Gallup Panel web survey, n=5,075 US adults aged 21+, March 20-April 6 2026, MOE +/-1.8: among adults who sought financial guidance in the past year (about three quarters of Americans), 18% used AI tools including ChatGPT, Claude and similar assistants, vs internet research 73%, family 35%, professional advisors 32%, news or social media 26%, friends 23% (Gallup 2026) | Same survey, confidence in each source's expertise in managing money: no more than three in ten adults have at least some confidence in AI and 3% in the US have a great deal; 79% have at least some confidence in financial advisors (Gallup 2026) | Same survey: about one in four Gen Z adults and millennials have used AI for financial guidance vs 7% of baby boomers; at least some confidence in AI tools is 36% of millennials, 32% of Gen Z, 27% of Gen X and 15% of boomers (Gallup 2026)
Implication: AI labs have already taken a share of the money-question task among younger customers, yet confidence in them is low, so a bank's accountable, human-backed AI has an opening on advice that it must claim before the habit hardens.
Caveats: Co-sponsored by Edward Jones, an advice firm with an interest in showing advisors outrank AI; fielded by Gallup with disclosed n, dates and weighting. The 18% base is guidance-seekers, not all adults (roughly 13% of all adults by derivation, not published). Exact question wording not printed on the page. Compares AI with human sources, not with a bank's own AI. About asking, not letting AI act.

Claim: In early 2024 only 5% of US adults said they used AI when making financial decisions, and identical financial statements labelled as coming from AI were trusted less or distrusted more than when labelled as coming from a financial professional on three of four topics.
Evidence: FINRA Investor Education Foundation, SSRS Opinion Panel (probability-based), n=1,033 US adults, February 16-19 2024, AAPOR3 response rate 2.4%, MOE +/-3.6; question: which of the following information sources do you use when making financial decisions: financial professionals 63%, friends and family 56%, financial management apps 25%, AI 5% (FINRA Foundation 2024) | Same study, randomised source label: portfolio allocation statement trusted by 37% when attributed to a financial professional vs 30% when attributed to AI; stock-bond forecast trusted about equally (33% vs 34%) but distrusted by 23% under the AI label vs 19% (FINRA Foundation 2024) | Same study, exceptions: Black respondents trusted the homeownership statement more when attributed to AI (71% vs 49%); respondents with higher self-assessed knowledge trusted the stock-bond forecast more from AI (48% vs 34%) (FINRA Foundation 2024)
Implication: As of early 2024 a bare AI label on financial information carried a small trust penalty, so a bank AI should be presented as backed by the bank and its people rather than as a standalone machine.
Caveats: Pre-dates the 2025-2026 jump in chatbot use (see T3-09 and T3-10), so the 5% figure is stale. The item says AI, not a named assistant or provider, and respondents saw hypothetical statements, not real chatbot output. Differences are modest and some are not significant (p 0.03 to 0.14). Very low response rate. Investor-protection funder. Previously verified by the fs-agent-landscape T5 pass; cited here for the AI-vs-professional comparison. The homeownership trust split (57% vs 65%) appears only as chart labels and is not cited.

Claim: In the UK in 2026, about a quarter of bank-account holders saw ChatGPT-type tools as a reliable source of financial advice and few would give AI real-time access to their bank data, while being offered by a provider they already trust was a minor reason to adopt financial AI.
