Evidence: Yonder Consulting for the FCA, online panel n=5,026 UK adults with a day-to-day bank account, April 2026, quota-representative; question A9: to what extent do AI-enabled tools like ChatGPT provide reliable financial information or advice: 26% completely or somewhat reliable; by age 30% (18-24), 37% (25-34), 35% (35-44) down to 13% (65-74) and 12% (75+) (FCA consumer research 2026; age values from chart labels) | Same survey, question A5: would you be willing to give an AI real-time access to your banking and financial data: 13% yes, 70% no among all consumers; 18% yes among current AI users; 16% already use AI to support personal finance (FCA consumer research 2026) | Same survey, question A4 (rank up to three triggers that would make you more likely to use AI for money): clear rules protecting me 32%, proven track record 30%, if it was offered by a financial services provider I already trust 13%, none of the above 24% (FCA consumer research 2026; values from chart labels, order cross-checked against the 24% printed in the summary) | Same survey, concept test: definitely or probably would use AI that reviews and recommends 36%, acts asking permission each time 30%, acts autonomously within pre-set goals 20%; only 40% know there is no formal recourse after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool; the FCA states it does not regulate such advice, so FSCS and FOS protection does not apply (FCA consumer research 2026; FCA InvestSmart page)
Implication: Protection and track record matter more to customers than who offers the AI, so a US bank's trust advantage for AI must be made concrete as recourse and liability rather than assumed from brand; the same research shows willingness falling as AI moves from recommending to acting.
Caveats: UK, not US; regulator-commissioned (the FCA has a perimeter agenda) and fielded by a consultancy on an online panel. Stated intention for hypothetical concepts, not behaviour. Several figures are chart data labels in the extracted PDF. The concept test mixes providers, so it is not a bank-vs-AI-lab comparison. The ask-vs-act gradient also bears on H1 (task-level trust). The press release is cited for context only; it does not repeat these survey figures.

Claim: UK current-account customers rarely switched banks in the mid-2010s, about 3% a year, with roughly two thirds neither searching nor switching over three years, and US account holders report keeping the same checking account for 19 years on average: the main banking relationship is behaviourally sticky whatever customers think of their bank.
Evidence: CMA retail banking market investigation, final report appendices (2016), citing GfK PCA consumer survey: 8% of UK personal current account customers switched within the last three years (England 8%, n=3,049; NI 7%, n=702; Scotland 7%, n=661) (CMA 2016) | Same appendix, GfK table: 78.1% neither searched nor switched in the last 12 months and 65.4% in the last three years (CMA 2016) | Same appendix: the CMA refers to an overall 3% annual switching rate and estimates switching through CASS and its predecessor at around 2% of all UK main accounts; it concludes that switching rates for UK PCA customers are low and that the rate has increased over time but still remains low (CMA 2016) | Same appendix: switching is lower for current accounts than for car insurance, savings accounts and energy (CMA 2016) | Bankrate survey fielded by YouGov, online non-probability panel with quotas and weights, n=2,712 US adults (2,058 with a checking account), January 27-29 2025: checking-account holders have kept the same account for an average of 19 years (19 years for accounts with branches, 6 years for online-only accounts); savings 17 years (18 branch, 6 online-only); boomers 28 years, Gen X 19, millennials 12, Gen Z 6; only about 1 in 4 checking and savings holders opened their accounts in the past five years (Bankrate 2025) | Same survey, reasons checking-account holders stay: 43% gave convenience reasons, including it's the account I've always had 18% and too much of a hassle to switch 9%; no/low monthly fees 18%; happy with customer service 16% (Bankrate 2025) | Bank of England Staff Working Paper 540 (2015), UK macro data: the elasticity of household deposits with respect to the interest rate paid is typically of the order of 0.3, i.e. retail deposits are rate-inelastic (BoE abstract) | NBER Working Paper 34742 (January 2026), account-level data on more than 12 million accounts at 154 US institutions, almost entirely credit unions, 2011-2023: 10% of depositors hold 70% of deposits; unlike low-balance households, high-balance retail depositors are not sensitive to interest-rate shocks, and overall retail deposit stickiness is driven by high-balance accounts used as liquidity stores (NBER 2026)
Implication: A bank holding the main account has time: even if attitudes toward its AI shift, account switching is slow, so the risk is erosion of tasks around the account rather than sudden loss of it.
Caveats: UK evidence is pre-AI, mid-2010s data. Shows inertia, not trust; the CMA treats low switching as a competition problem, not evidence of satisfaction, so stickiness can coexist with distrust. Switching tools and open banking have changed the UK market since. Recovery-pass additions: Bankrate is a consumer-finance publisher's non-probability survey (flagged, Low on its own) and measures tenure, not switching rate; the shorter tenure for online-only accounts and Gen Z (6 years) fits those products and cohorts being new but also shows the young hold accounts at newer institutions. The BoE figure is from the abstract only and is a decade old. The NBER paper is an unreviewed working paper on credit-union data supplied by a bank-software vendor (nCino), not large banks, and finds low-balance households are rate-sensitive. Vintage kept at the CMA data year. No independent US annual switching rate was verified (J.D. Power primary blocked; see gaps).

Claim: Confidence in banks across the 25 countries hit hardest by the 2008 crisis fell by 20 points, did not approach its pre-crisis level until 2020 and reached a new high in 2025, but the United States is among the countries still at least 14 points below its pre-crisis peak.
Evidence: Gallup World Poll, confidence in financial institutions and banks, median of 25 most-affected countries: 57% before the crisis, 40% in 2009, record low 37% in 2012, 56% in 2020, 63% in 2025 (new high) (Gallup 2026) | Same release: nine countries remain at least five points below pre-crash levels, including Belgium, Spain, Greece and the United States, all of which posted 2025 scores at least 14 points below their pre-crash peaks (Gallup 2026) | Same release: Gallup links the recovery to how comfortable people feel living on their household income rather than to regulatory reform alone; fieldwork March 27-December 5 2025, about 1,000 adults per country, MOE +/-2.2 to 5.5 (Gallup 2026)
Implication: Institutional trust in banks can be rebuilt after a systemic shock, but slowly and on the back of household economics, and not yet in the US, so a bank should treat trust lost to an AI failure as a decade-scale problem rather than a quarter-scale one.
Caveats: Independent pollster. Cross-country median, not US-only; the US detail is a single sentence. Institutional trust, not trust in bank AI, and says nothing about fintech or big tech. Correction from slice: the slice said only that the US was at least five points lower; the page places the US in the group at least 14 points below its pre-crash peak.

Claim: US trust that businesses will use AI responsibly reversed within a year, falling from 31% in 2025 to 27% in 2026 after two years of gains, with the sharpest fall among adults aged 18 to 29.
Evidence: Bentley-Gallup Business in Society survey, Gallup Panel web study, n=3,270 US adults, May 4-11 2026, MOE +/-2.4: 27% trust businesses a lot or some to use AI responsibly, down from 31% in 2025; Gallup says this halted two years of gradual improvement and remains somewhat higher than 2023 and 2024 (Gallup 2026) | Same survey: among adults aged 18-29, at least some trust fell from 30% to 20% and those with no trust at all rose from 29% to 41% (Gallup 2026) | Same survey: share saying AI does more harm than good rose from 31% in 2025 to 39% in 2026 (40% in 2023); among 18-29s it rose to 47% from 36%; 79% expect AI to reduce US jobs over 10 years, up from 73% (Gallup 2026)
Implication: Attitudes toward business use of AI move year to year and are falling fastest among the young, so a bank should treat today's comfort with its AI as provisional and design agentic features so a sentiment swing does not strand them.
Caveats: Asks about businesses in general, not banks or financial tasks, and about attitude, not behaviour; it shows volatility of AI attitudes, not migration between providers. The overall 4-point move is modest; the 18-29 drop is a subgroup estimate. University partner (Bentley), no AI-vendor sponsor. Previously verified by the fs-agent-landscape T5 pass; cited here for its durability implication.

Claim: In the Federal Reserve's payment diaries US consumers made half of person-to-person payments through mobile apps in 2023 and 45% of remote payments by phone in 2024, but the Fed reports that mobile payment app use has been stable and attributes the rise in phone payments to card and ACH payments made through the phone.
Evidence: Federal Reserve Financial Services, 2024 Findings from the Diary of Consumer Payment Choice (October 2023 diary): consumers used mobile apps for 50% of person-to-person payments (Fed 2024 findings page) | 2025 Findings from the Diary of Consumer Payment Choice (October 2024 diary; 5,583 individuals from the USC Understanding America Study panel, weighted to Census CPS estimates): mobile phones were used for 23% of all payments, 11% of in-person non-bill payments and 45% of remote payments; adults 18-24 used a phone for 45% of all payments; consumers made an average of 11 phone payments a month in 2024, up from 10 in 2023 (Fed 2025 findings) | Same report, footnotes: mobile payment apps are defined as PayPal, Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, MoneyGram and similar; Figure 1 shows mobile payment app use has been stable, and the increase in phone use is due to people choosing to make card or ACH payments with their phone rather than with the card itself or a pre-loaded app balance; a card payment made via a phone is classified as a card payment (Fed 2025 findings) | Atlanta Fed 2023 Survey and Diary of Consumer Payment Choice (published June 2024), abstract: 72 percent of consumers adopted online or mobile payment accounts like PayPal, Zelle, Venmo and Cash App in 2023, and 73 percent used mobile banking (Fed in Print abstract)
Implication: Payments moved to phone and app interfaces, largely running on bank cards and ACH, so a bank should expect customers to hand payment tasks to an AI on a non-bank surface while the funding account stays at the bank, and should compete for the interface as well as the ledger.
Caveats: Diary data from a probability-based panel fielded by the Fed; no sponsor interest. Adoption, not trust, and nothing about AI. The app category includes Zelle, a bank-owned network, so app use cannot be read as nonbank share. The Fed's stable statement refers to its multi-year chart, not to a printed series, and no year-by-year app share before 2023 was verified (Atlanta Fed report PDFs blocked), so this row establishes a level, not a trend. The 2023 diary sample size is not on the page. The Atlanta Fed 72% and 73% figures come from an abstract read through WebFetch, not the report body, so question wording is unverified.

Claim: In the Fed's SHED 94% of US adults had a bank account in both 2022 and 2025, nonbank check cashing and money orders fell to 12% of adults by 2025, and crypto payments stayed at 1-2%, while buy now, pay later rose from 12% of adults (2022) to 16% (2025): the account relationship held while one credit task moved.
Evidence: Fed Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking 2025 (fielded October 2025, final sample 12,934 adults): 94 percent of adults had a bank account; 12 percent used nonbank check cashing or money orders, similar to recent years and down 4 percentage points from 2019; 11 percent of banked vs 28 percent of unbanked adults used them (SHED 2025 report) | Same report, Table 33 (among all adults, 2021/2022/2023/2024/2025): used cryptocurrency to buy something or make a payment 2/2/1/2/2%; to send money to friends or family 1/2/1/1/1%; any use 12/10/7/8/10%. Table 34: among adults who used crypto for transactions, don't trust banks was the main reason for 7% (SHED 2025 report) | Same report: BNPL use edged up 1 percentage point to 16 percent of all adults; 11 percent of BNPL users had a payment trigger an overdraft or NSF fee from their bank. SHED 2022-data fact sheet (May 2023): 94 percent of adults had a bank account in 2022 and 12 percent used BNPL in the prior year (SHED 2025 report; SHED 2023 fact sheet) | Same 2025 report, Table 37: peer-to-peer payments (such as Zelle, PayPal, Venmo, CashApp or Apple Cash) were the payment method in 29% of non-credit-card fraud, behind debit cards 41% (SHED 2025 report)
Implication: Account ownership is not migrating, so a bank can plan AI rollout on a stable account base, but BNPL shows a nonbank can take a discrete credit task within three years, which is the pattern to expect for AI-delegated tasks.
Caveats: Regulator survey with disclosed method (online probability panel; the report notes it may under-represent the less connected). Ownership, not primacy: 94% says nothing about which institution is primary. Behaviour, not trust, and nothing about AI (SHED's only generative AI item is workplace use). Don't trust banks is asked only of crypto transactors. No provider split for BNPL in the text. SHED has no item on P2P use or on trust in nonbank providers in the 2022-2025 editions extracted. The 2022 fact sheet gives crypto for transactions as 3%, a combined measure, while the 2025 table splits it into two items. The recovery researcher filed this Contradicts; BNPL growth makes Mixed the honest reading.

Claim: In a March 2024 survey of 2,000 Canadians, the share somewhat or very likely to share financial data under open banking was 35% for large international banks, 30% for small Canadian institutions, 27% for Canadian fintechs, 20% for large tech companies and 13% for social media platforms.
Evidence: Environics Research, March 2024, 2,000 Canadians; respondents were told consumer-led data control lets them direct financial data such as transaction history and credit scores to third-party financial institutions to access better products; 45% supported authorising their financial institution to transfer their data to third parties (Environics write-up) | Same survey, somewhat or very likely to share data with: large international banks with offices in Canada (example given: American Express) 35%; small licensed Canadian financial institutions 30%; Canadian fintechs (Borrowell, Wealthsimple) 27%; large tech companies (Google, Amazon) 20%; large mobile companies (Samsung, Google) 20%; social media platforms (Facebook, LinkedIn) 13% (Environics write-up)
Implication: Even in a recent open-banking setting a bank recipient beats fintech by only 8 points and big tech by 15, so the bank data-trust edge is real but too small to treat as protected.
Caveats: Sponsor, fieldwork mode, weighting, margin of error and exact question wording are not disclosed in the write-up; Low for that reason. Stated intention about data sharing, not AI. Category examples are odd (American Express as a large international bank) and Canada's big domestic banks are not a listed recipient, so the bank category is not the respondent's own bank. Canadian data in a concentrated banking market; transfer to the US uncertain. Agrees in direction with the US 2020 NY Fed ranking (T3-01). An earlier Ipsos Canada poll (Aug-Oct 2018, n=1,000 chequing-account holders) found 6 in 10 trust their banks to provide open banking but asked no comparator, so it is not cited.

Claim: US concern about AI in daily life rose in one step around ChatGPT (2022 to 2023) and has stayed flat at 50-52% since. Adults under 30 are the exception: their concern kept rising every wave after 2024, and by 2026 they had moved from the least concerned age group to level with adults 65 and older.
Evidence: Pew Research Center, US adults, 'the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life makes you feel more concerned than excited / equally concerned and excited / more excited than concerned': more concerned 37% (2021), 38% (2022), 52% (2023), 51% (2024), 50% (2025; n=5,023, June 9-15, 2025), 52% (2026; n=3,488, June 22-28, 2026); more excited 18% (2021) to 9% (2026) | Same item, ages 18-29 more concerned: 31% (2021), 29% (2022), 42% (2023), 39% (2024), 47% (2025), 55% (2026); ages 65+: 43%, 45%, 61%, 59%, 56%, 59% (Pew 2026 data table) | Same item, ages 50-64: 41% (2021), 59% (2023), 47% (2026); ages 30-49: 34% (2021), 48% (2023), 51% (2026); ages 18-29 more excited than concerned 25% (2021) to 11% (2026). Pew: for ages 30+ the rise came mainly in the first two years, while under-30 concern continues to climb
Implication: Do not plan on younger customers replacing older ones to lift AI sentiment. The youngest adults are now as wary as the oldest, so a US bank has to earn trust for each task itself.
Caveats: Pew is non-profit and independent, using a probability-based panel (American Trends Panel). The item measures concern versus excitement about AI in daily life (an affect measure); it does not ask about trust, banking or any financial task. Values for 2021-2024 come from the data table printed on Pew's 2026 page and match the 2021 and 2025 figures printed in the 2025 report text. The waves are repeated cross-sections, so cohort and period effects cannot be separated. Concern among 50-64s fell 12 points from 2023 to 2026, so the picture is not wariness rising at every age. Merged from slices T4-A (whole population) and T4-B (age splits).

Claim: Awareness of AI and use of AI both rose sharply in the US and in a 17-country panel without any fall in concern or worry. Exposure alone has not produced rising trust so far.
Evidence: Pew, US adults who have heard or read 'a lot' about AI: 26% (2022) to 47% (2025; n=5,023, June 9-15, 2025), up 7 points in the last year and 21 since 2022 (text); intermediate chart labels 33% (2023), 40% (2024). Over the same period 'more concerned than excited' went from 38% (2022) to 50% (2025) | Bentley University-Gallup, US adults: 70% say they are somewhat or extremely knowledgeable about AI in 2026, up from 64% in 2024, while 'AI does more harm than good' went from 31% (2024 and 2025) to 39% (2026); n=3,270, May 4-11, 2026 | KPMG/University of Melbourne, 17 countries surveyed in late 2022 and in 2024: employees reporting intentional use of AI at work rose from 54% to 67%, while the share worried about AI systems rose from 49% to 62% (separate source, not combined)
Implication: A bank should not count on general familiarity with AI to raise trust in its own AI. Trust has to come from how its features perform, the control they give customers, and the recourse available when something goes wrong.
Caveats: The evidence is two series moving at the same time, not a causal test. All three sources are repeated cross-sections, and awareness is not use. KPMG sells AI advisory and assurance services, so it has an interest in a 'trust gap' headline; its academic lead is the University of Melbourne. The Pew values for 2023 and 2024 awareness are chart labels; only the 2022 and 2025 values and the change statements are printed text. None of the items is about finance. Originally tagged H2 (familiarity as a driver) in slice T4-A and re-tagged Projection here.

Claim: Among all US adults, trust in businesses to use AI responsibly rose from 2023 to 2025 and dipped in 2026, but it remains above its 2023 level. The share saying AI does more harm than good fell and then returned to its 2023 level. The all-adult series is a round trip, not a steady slide.
Evidence: Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society survey, US adults 18+, trust businesses 'a lot' or 'some' to use AI responsibly: 21% (2023), 23% (2024), 31% (2025), 27% (2026; n=3,270, May 4-11, 2026, margin of error about 2.4 points) | Same survey, 'AI does more harm than good': 40% (2023), 31% (2024), 31% (2025), 39% (2026); 'more good than harm' 10%, 13%, 12%, 9% | Same survey, expect AI to reduce the total number of US jobs: 75% (2023), 75% (2024), 73% (2025), 79% (2026)
Implication: The US baseline is a low and volatile plateau: about one in four adults extends trust to business use of AI. A bank should expect sentiment to move with news events and should not read one good year as a trend.
Caveats: Fielded by Gallup for Bentley University, both academic or independent organisations. The item asks about 'businesses' in general, not banks. This is four waves of repeated cross-sections. Gallup frames 2026 as a cooling after two years of improving attitudes. Earlier T4 notes described a '21% to 31% to 27%' trajectory, and the full printed series is 21/23/31/27. Trust in 2026 (27%) is still higher than in 2023 (21%), so it is not correct to describe this series as falling over the period.

Claim: US adults aged 18-29 moved sharply against business use of AI in 2026. Their trust fell, the share saying AI does more harm than good rose for the second year running to the highest of any age group, and the youngest group is no longer the most positive.
Evidence: Bentley University-Gallup, ages 18-29, trust businesses at least some to use AI responsibly: 30% (2025) to 20% (2026); 'none at all' 29% to 41% (all adults n=3,270, May 4-11, 2026) | Same survey, ages 18-29, 'AI does more harm than good': 30% (2023), 27% (2024), 36% (2025), 47% (2026); Gallup says the 11-point rise from 2025 to 2026 was the largest of any age group | Same survey, ages 18-29 expecting AI to reduce US jobs in the next decade: 62% (2025) to 75% (2026)
Implication: Do not treat digital-native customers as a ready base of early adopters for bank AI. On recent trend they are the age group moving fastest toward scepticism.
Caveats: Bentley University-Gallup is independent. Gallup does not publish the n for the 18-29 subsample, so year-on-year changes carry a wider margin than the overall 2.4 points. The trust item has only two youth waves in the page text; the harm-versus-good item has four, and it rises only over the last two. The item covers businesses in general, not banks. The result points the same way as the Pew under-30 series (row T4-01) but comes from a different survey; the two are not combined.

Claim: For one finance-specific task, receiving a financial-advice recommendation, the share of US adults who say AI performs worse than a person fell between 2023 and 2026. The people who left that answer moved to 'same as a person', not to 'better'. It is the only finance task in this set where a repeated measure moved toward acceptance.
Evidence: Bentley University-Gallup, US adults, how AI performs compared with a person at 'Recommend financial advice to me': worse than a person 49% (2023) to 43% (2026); same as a person 36% to 42%; better than a person 15% to 15% (2026 n=3,270, May 4-11, 2026) | Same table, 'Recommend medical advice to me': better than a person 11% (2023) to 12% (2026); Gallup says AI is still judged worse than people on all tasks asked about in 2023 and 2026 | Gallup/Edward Jones (separate survey, not combined): 79% of US adults have at least some confidence in the expertise of financial advisors versus no more than three in ten for AI as a source of financial guidance (n=5,075 adults 21+, March 20-April 6, 2026)
Implication: The movement is toward parity with humans, not preference for AI. A bank can expect AI recommendations to become acceptable more slowly than they become preferred, and keeping a human option available stays important for advice.
Caveats: There are only two waves, three years apart, and the 6-point move is modest. The figures come from a data table embedded in the Gallup page; Gallup's text does not print the full question stem. 'Recommend financial advice' does not name a bank or say whether the AI acts. The Gallup/Edward Jones study is sponsored by Edward Jones, which sells human financial advice and has an interest in showing confidence in advisors. Gallup fielded it.

Claim: In single-wave surveys from the US (2026) and the UK (2026), confidence in AI as a source of money guidance is higher among younger adults than older ones. Cohort replacement would therefore lift the average. The gradient peaks among people in their late 20s and 30s, not the youngest, and even the peak is only about one in three.
Evidence: Gallup/Edward Jones, US adults 21+ (n=5,075, March 20-April 6, 2026), at least some confidence in AI tools as a source of expertise on managing money: millennials 36%, Gen Z 32%, Gen X 27%, baby boomers 15%; 3% of all adults have a great deal; about one in four Gen Z and millennials used AI for financial guidance versus 7% of boomers (18% of guidance seekers overall) | FCA/Yonder, UK adults with a day-to-day bank account (n=5,026, April 2026), AI tools like ChatGPT 'provide reliable financial information or advice', completely or somewhat reliable by age: 18-24 30%, 25-34 37%, 35-44 35%, 45-54 29%, 55-64 21%, 65-74 13%, 75+ 12% (chart labels) | Pew, US adults who ever use AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot: 18-29 55% (2024) to 66% (2026), 30-49 41% to 61%, 50-64 25% to 42%, 65+ 12% to 23% (n=5,119, Feb 17-23, 2026; 2024 wording differed and was asked only of those aware of chatbots)
Implication: Replacing older cohorts would raise average confidence in AI money guidance, but only to a ceiling of about one in three. Use is rising faster than confidence across all ages, so a bank should expect customers to use AI without trusting it much.
Caveats: These are cross-sectional age splits, not trends. Under-30s are trending more negative on general AI (rows T4-01 and T4-04), so the age gradient may not hold. Edward Jones sponsored the Gallup study and sells advice. Gen Z in that study is 21+ only, and the Gen Z versus millennial gap is probably within sampling error. The Yonder values are chart data labels mapped to age bands in printed order; they are UK figures and were commissioned by the FCA. Pew measures use, not trust. The two surveys are separate and not combined. An earlier Fed SHED item (workers' generative AI use at work) was removed as off-measure.

Claim: Across 17 countries surveyed in both late 2022 and 2024, every headline trust measure fell and worry rose: perceived trustworthiness of AI systems, willingness to rely on AI, and the view that benefits outweigh risks.
Evidence: KPMG/University of Melbourne, 17 countries in both waves, 'perceive AI systems as trustworthy' (somewhat agree or higher): 63% (2022) to 56% (2024), lower in 13 of 17 countries | Same, 'willing to rely on AI systems' (somewhat willing or higher): 52% to 43%, lower in 12 of 17 countries | Same, 'worried about AI systems' (moderately, very or extremely): 49% to 62%, higher in 15 of 17; 'benefits of AI outweigh the risks': 50% to 41%. The 2024 study covered 48,340 respondents across 47 countries; the 2022 wave included the USA
Implication: In the only multi-country series that measures trust in AI itself, trust fell while use rose. A bank should not assume that trust follows adoption.
Caveats: KPMG sells AI advisory and assurance services and benefits from a 'trust gap' headline; the University of Melbourne ran the research. The 2022 wave was fielded just before ChatGPT's release, so the change is partly a before-and-after-ChatGPT step. The samples are independent cross-sections, and some measures were modified between waves (the report recalculated composites on shared items only and says changes are indicative). Comparisons cover only three applications (AI in general, healthcare, HR). This is a 17-country average, not US-specific. The direction disagrees with Ipsos's rising benefits item (row T4-08).

Claim: In Ipsos's multi-country monitor, nervousness about AI products jumped between the pre-ChatGPT wave and 2023 and has been roughly flat since at about 52-53%. Over the same period the view that AI products have more benefits than drawbacks kept rising, and trust that AI companies will protect personal data held at just under half.
Evidence: Ipsos, agree 'Products and services using artificial intelligence make me nervous': 52% in 2023 (31 countries, n=22,816 adults under 75, May 26-June 9, 2023), an average 12-point rise across 24 countries since the December 2021 survey (Ipsos page); Stanford AI Index 2024 describes it as a 13-point rise from 2022 | Ipsos AI Monitor 2025 (n=23,216 online adults under 75, 30 countries, March 21-April 4, 2025): 30-country average 53% nervous (chart label), described as 'mostly flat year over year but still quite a bit up from 2022'; Stanford AI Index 2026 text gives 52% in 2025, 'up 2 percentage points' in one passage and '+3' in another | Agree AI products and services have more benefits than drawbacks: 52% (2022) to 55% (2024) per Stanford AI Index 2025 (26 nations in both waves), and 55% (2024) to 59% (2025) per Stanford AI Index 2026 | Trust that companies using AI will protect personal data: 50% (2023) to 47% (2024) per Stanford AI Index 2025; 48% (2025) per Ipsos
Implication: Wariness is stable and perceived benefit is drifting upward. A bank should plan for an ambivalent, roughly steady baseline rather than either a continued slide or a recovery.
Caveats: Ipsos is an independent research firm, and the monitor is not sponsored by an AI vendor. The country set changes between waves (24, 26, 30 and 31 countries), and the averages are unweighted country means of online samples that skew urban and educated in emerging markets. The baseline for the jump is the December 2021 fieldwork according to Ipsos and '2022' according to Stanford; the sources print +12 and +13 points respectively for different country sets, and no pre-ChatGPT level is printed in the fetched text, so none is stated here. Stanford prints both +2 and +3 for the 2024-2025 change in nervousness. The 2025 values of 52% (Stanford) and 53% (Ipsos 30-country chart label) come from different presentations and are kept separate. A US value for 2023 (32% trust companies to protect data) was not found on the cited page and was removed. Not about banking.

Claim: The best-case banking-technology analogue is slow. Mobile banking as the primary way US households access their bank account took about six years to become the most common method and ten years to reach 48%. It never reached a majority, and branch and ATM channels were not displaced. Adoption rose at every age in the same years, which points to a shared period effect, while the age gap persisted.
Evidence: FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households (Census CPS supplement), banked households, mobile banking as primary method of account access: 34.0% (2019), 43.5% (2021), 48.3% (2023) (text); 5.5% (2013), 9.2% (2015), 15.1% (2017) (chart labels); FDIC text: 'almost ninefold' over the decade and the most prevalent method since 2019 | Same, bank teller as primary method 33.3% (2013) to 14.9% (2023) (chart labels; FDIC text: 'fell by more than half'); in 2023, 70.5% used an off-site channel as primary, and almost all banked households still used an ATM or teller at least once | Same, by age of householder, mobile as primary: FDIC text says 'almost sixfold' for ages 25-34 and 'more than 30-fold' for 65+; chart labels 15-24: 19.7% (2013) to 76.6% (2023); 25-34: 12.8% to 74.8%; 65+: 0.6% to 19.3%
Implication: Plan AI as an additional channel that gains share over years and has to work for customers of all ages, not as a replacement that wins by default. Even mobile, which offered a clear convenience payoff, needed a decade to reach under half as the primary channel.
Caveats: This is a federal survey conducted by Census for the FDIC. The 2013, 2015 and 2017 yearly values and all values by age were read from the printed chart data labels in the PDF, not from a table: they are chart-read. The age mapping follows label order and is consistent with FDIC's printed 'sixfold' and '30-fold' statements. The 2019-2023 overall values are in the report text. The unit is the household, by age of householder. 'Primary method' is mutually exclusive, so wider use was higher. Mobile banking is a channel, not AI, and the survey does not measure trust. Merged from slices T4-B (by age) and T4-C (whole population).

Claim: In the Federal Reserve's mobile surveys, mobile banking use roughly doubled in four years even though most non-users still cited security concern. The main barrier was 'no need', not distrust, and users rated it far safer than non-users did. Adoption came before stated trust, not after it.
Evidence: Federal Reserve Board, Consumers and Mobile Financial Services 2016 (GfK KnowledgePanel, n=2,510, fieldwork Nov 2015): mobile phone owners with a bank account who used mobile banking in the past 12 months 22% (2011), 33% (2013), 39% (2014), 43% (2015); smartphone owners with a bank account 43% (2011) to 53% (2015) | Same, reasons for non-use among non-users (multiple yes/no): banking needs met without it 88%; no reason to use 78%; concerned about security 73%; screen too small 43%; 'I don't trust the technology' 40%; 54% of non-users had no interest in any mobile banking activity even if their concerns were addressed | Fed mobile security page, 2015, mobile phone owners (n=2,244): mobile banking very safe 8%, somewhat safe 35%, somewhat unsafe 24%, very unsafe 18%, don't know 15%; 71% of mobile banking users rated it safe versus 25% of non-users; convenience (39%) and getting a smartphone (26%) were the main reasons people started
Implication: Uptake of a new banking channel was driven by convenience and device ownership while stated security fear stayed high. A bank should expect AI adoption to follow a clear payoff and early use, and should not wait for stated distrust to disappear first.
Caveats: This is a Federal Reserve survey with no commercial sponsor. It used an online probability panel in English only, and the 2011 wave was built differently (the report notes limits on comparability). The safety item is a single 2015 wave; the user/non-user gap is cross-sectional and could reflect self-selection. Non-use reasons overlap. The data predate generative AI and are mechanism evidence only. No later waves of this series were located.

Claim: Mobile phone payments in US stores grew steadily but remain a minority behaviour. Consumers of all ages more than doubled in-person phone payments after 2020, yet in 2024 phones accounted for 11% of in-person payments and 95% of consumers still preferred cards or cash.
Evidence: Federal Reserve Financial Services / Atlanta and Boston Feds, 2025 Findings from the Diary of Consumer Payment Choice (5,583 participants, October 2024 diary): mobile phones used for 23% of all payments, 11% of in-person non-bill payments and 45% of remote payments in 2024 | Same, average mobile phone payments per consumer 10 (2023) to 11 (2024); consumers of all ages more than doubled in-person mobile phone payments compared with 2020; ages 18-24 used phones for 45% of all payments | Same, non-cash share of in-person payments 60% (2016) to 78% (2024); 95% favoured debit cards, credit cards or cash for in-person payments in 2024; more than 94% still used cash as a primary instrument, backup or store of value
Implication: A new way to pay can stay a growing minority habit for most of a decade. A US bank should expect AI-initiated or delegated payments to sit alongside existing instruments for years rather than replace them.
Caveats: The publisher is a Federal Reserve unit that also provides payment services; the report is descriptive. 'Mobile phone payment' is the device the respondent reports using and is not a clean measure of contactless wallet use. Only the 2016, 2020, 2023 and 2024 comparisons printed in the text are used. The 95% preference item is a single wave. This is a payments analogue, not AI, and it does not measure trust.

Claim: The UK regulator's own consumer survey finds that stated willingness to use AI in personal finance falls as autonomy rises, from 36% for recommendations to 20% for autonomous action. Willingness is higher among people who already use AI, but a segment rejects every level. The FCA's 2030 review names trust, control and access as preconditions for adopting AI finance agents and gives no numerical forecast.
Evidence: FCA-commissioned Yonder survey, UK adults with a day-to-day bank account (n=5,026, April 2026), 'How likely would you be to use something like this, if it were available to you now?', definitely or probably use: 36% (AI reviews data and recommends), 30% (AI can take action, asking permission each time), 20% (AI takes autonomous actions on pre-set instructions or goals) | Same, among existing AI users (n=3,473): 48%, 40%, 28%; 16% of consumers already use AI for personal finance; 13% would give AI real-time access to banking data; 24% say nothing would persuade them to use AI in financial services | FCA Mills Review (published 6 July 2026): the central shift to 2030 is toward services that are 'AI-enabled, continuous and delegated', and its consumer research found that trust, control and access must be right before consumers adopt AI finance agents. The review is qualitative and contains no numerical adoption forecast
Implication: Each step up in autonomy costs about a sixth to nearly half of stated willingness. A US bank should launch delegated AI at recommend-and-confirm, build recourse in, and not assume that the mobile-banking adoption curve applies to agents.
Caveats: This is stated intention toward hypothetical concepts in one UK wave. The projection rests on a cross-sectional comparison of AI users with all respondents; Yonder itself frames this both as a sign that willingness could grow with familiarity and as evidence that 'exposure alone may not overcome resistance'. Respondents each saw one of five concept sets in sequence, so the levels mix topics and order effects are possible. The survey was conducted for the regulator as input to its review. Transfer to the US is an inference: Reg E and chargeback rights differ. The same survey appears in other topics; it is kept here only for the autonomy-level projection.
